title: The South African livestock farming environment

lessons.title: Livestock farming in South Africa
lessons.html:
Livestock farming in South Africa

Livestock farming is one of the biggest parts of farming in South Africa. Most of our land is too dry for crops. But grass and bushes grow on it, and animals can eat them. So farmers keep animals on this land.

The main animals

  • Cattle for beef and milk. Beef cattle often run on veld. Dairy cows are milked every day.
  • Sheep for meat (mutton and lamb) and wool. Merino and Dohne Merino are wool sheep. Dorper is a meat sheep.
  • Goats for meat, milk and mohair. Boer goats are meat goats. Angora goats give mohair.
  • Pigs for pork. Most pigs are kept in houses.
  • Poultry for eggs and chicken meat.

Where animals are farmed

Different areas suit different animals. The Karoo is dry, so many farmers keep sheep and goats there. The sweetveld and bushveld areas carry beef cattle and game. The wetter areas in KwaZulu-Natal, the Eastern Cape coast and the Western Cape are good for dairy farms. Pigs and chickens can be farmed in many places, because they live in houses and eat bought feed.

Who farms livestock

There are big commercial farms with thousands of animals. There are also many small-scale and communal farmers. In communal areas, families share grazing land and bring animals to the kraal at night. Cattle are also important in many cultures for lobola and ceremonies.

All of these farmers need people who know how to look after animals. That is the work you are learning to do.

lessons.title: Farming systems and the natural environment
lessons.html:
Farming systems and the natural environment

Extensive and intensive farming

There are two main ways to farm animals.

ExtensiveIntensive
Animals graze on veld in big campsAnimals are kept in houses, pens or feedlots
Few animals per hectareMany animals in a small space
Mostly natural grazingMostly bought feed
Example: beef cattle in the bushveldExample: broiler houses, piggery, feedlot

Weather and climate

South Africa has dry years and wet years. Drought is a big risk. In a drought, the veld does not grow and water dries up. Farmers must sell animals or buy feed. Very hot days can stress animals. Cold, wet wind can kill newborn lambs. Watch the weather and tell your supervisor when it changes.

Looking after the veld

The veld is the farmer's most important resource. If too many animals graze one camp for too long, the good grass dies. Then bare soil washes away in the rain. This is called overgrazing and erosion. Farmers move animals between camps so the grass can rest and grow again.

The Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 is the law that protects farm soil and veld. Water use is controlled by the National Water Act 36 of 1998.

What you can do

  • Close gates so animals stay in the right camp.
  • Report leaking troughs and broken pipes.
  • Report bare patches, dongas and new weeds.
  • Never start fires in the veld.

Seasons on the farm

Summer is the rainy season in most of the country. The grass grows and animals gain weight. Winter is dry in most areas. The grass turns brown and has less food value, so animals may need a lick. Learn the seasons on your farm and what work happens in each one.

lessons.title: Rules, markets and your place on the farm
lessons.html:
Rules, markets and your place on the farm

Laws that protect animals and people

Some laws you should know about:

  • Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 says you may not be cruel to animals. Do not beat, starve or overload them.
  • Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984 deals with dangerous diseases like foot-and-mouth disease. Some diseases must be reported to the state vet.
  • Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 makes sure meat sold to people is safe.
  • OHS Act 85 of 1993 protects workers from injury.

Where the animals go

Animals are sold in different ways. Some go to auctions. Some go to feedlots to be fattened. Some go straight to the abattoir. Milk goes to a dairy factory. Wool goes to a broker. The price the farmer gets depends on the animal's weight, condition and health. A thin or sick animal sells for less money.

Identification and records

Animals must be marked so people know who owns them. Farmers use ear tags, tattoos and brand marks. The farmer must keep records of births, deaths, treatments and sales. Stock theft is a big problem in South Africa. Good marks and counts help to stop it.

Your role

Every worker helps the farm make money. You count animals, check water, watch for sick animals and report problems quickly. Be on time. Follow safety rules. Ask when you do not know.

Key points

  • Cattle, sheep, goats, pigs and poultry are the main farm animals in South Africa.
  • Extensive farming uses veld; intensive farming uses houses and bought feed.
  • Overgrazing kills good grass and causes erosion.
  • The law protects animals from cruelty and controls dangerous diseases.
  • Animals must be marked and counted, and records must be kept.
